opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that one's a bit of a personal favorite. The setup is simple: you start in this sleek, slightly futuristic office in Tokyo, with desks, a big window, and city lights outside. Then the prompt basically says to walk toward the window, and somewhere along the way the scene transitions into a dense jungle.

What I love about it is that it shows off a few things at once that are really hard for a world model.

First, it's interactive and real-time. Nobody pre-rendered a video of that transition. You're actually moving through the space, and the model generates each frame in response to what you do. Making it feel like you're walking from one place into a completely different one, rather than watching a cut, is a big deal.

Second, consistency. If you look away from something and then look back, it's still there. The desk is where you left it, and the plants that started creeping in are still creeping in. We don't have an explicit 3D representation under the hood, so that memory emerges from the model itself. Seeing it hold together across such a dramatic change in the scene was really encouraging for us.

And third, it captures the kind of creative, dreamlike quality that I think makes world models exciting beyond pure simulation. It isn't just reproducing the real world faithfully. It's letting you go somewhere that couldn't exist, where an office turns into a rainforest, and it still feels physically coherent while you're in it. The lighting changes, the foliage behaves plausibly, and the sense of space carries over.

So for me it's a nice microcosm of the whole project. It's realistic enough to be believable, flexible enough to be imaginative, and stable enough that you can actually spend time in it. That's exactly the combination we need if we want these models to eventually be useful environments for training agents, not just cool demos.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so that one's my favorite for a couple of reasons. The first is just that it's a really good illustration of what the model can actually do that the previous versions couldn't. So in that demo you start out in this sort of futuristic Tokyo office space, very clean, glass, neon, that kind of aesthetic, and then you step out through a door and you're suddenly in a jungle. And the interesting thing isn't really either of those environments on their own, it's the transition between them. Because the model has to maintain consistency across two completely different visual worlds while you're moving between them in real time, and it has to do that without anyone having built a 3D asset for either of them. There's no explicit world model there, no mesh, no physics engine. It's just the model predicting the next frame given your actions and everything that's come before.

The second reason is that it captures something about the promptability side, which is a big part of what's new in Genie 3. The jungle isn't something the model just decided to show you, it's something that was prompted into the world as it was running. So you're in this office and you say, essentially, "okay, now a jungle," and the world adapts. And it does it in a way that still feels coherent. The lighting makes sense, the way you move through the space makes sense, if you turn around the office is still there behind you. That's the memory piece, the fact that it's able to hold onto what it's already generated for long enough that you can look away and look back and things are where you left them.

And honestly the third reason is just that it's fun. I think people sometimes look at these demos and want the hard technical argument, and there is one, but part of what made me excited about it is that it's the kind of thing you'd never bother building by hand. Nobody is going to go and model a Tokyo office that opens onto a rainforest. But if you can just say it and then be in it, that's a different relationship with the thing. It's less like a tool and more like a place you can go. And that's really where I think a lot of the value is going to come from, both for agents learning in these environments and for people just experiencing them.

astra-6.text: What I love about that example is the contrast between the futuristic Tokyo office and the jungle. They’re very different environments, and putting them together makes the creative possibilities feel tangible. You’re not just looking at an interesting image—you’re exploring a world. For me, that’s the exciting part: the sense that you can take an imaginative idea and turn it into somewhere you can actually move around.

sol-6.1.text: What I love about that example is the contrast. You’ve got this futuristic Tokyo office, and then this lush jungle—two very different environments that invite you to explore. It captures the appeal of a world model: you’re not just watching a scene unfold, you’re deciding where to go and seeing how the world responds. That makes it feel much more like a place you can inhabit than a video you’re watching.
